name: metadata-mapping
intent: Holds the correspondence between object fields and database columns in metadata - annotations, mapping files, table objects, struct tags or a schema definition - so that one generic mapping engine performs the reads, inserts and updates instead of hand-written per-class mapper code.
problem: Every class that is persisted needs the same tedious, repetitive code: which field maps to which column, which key is generated, how nulls and types convert, what the table is called. Written per class it is duplicated everywhere and drifts from the schema; the catalogue's trigger is that the mapping knowledge belongs in metadata or configuration, duplicated in no class.
context: Object-relational (or object-document) mapping layers where classes and tables do not line up mechanically - renamed columns, generated keys, relationships, inheritance strategies - and where many classes share the same mapping shape. It applies when the mapping can be declared once in a form a machine can read (code annotations or attributes, external XML, code-first table objects, struct tags, a schema DSL) and when the schema can either be generated from that metadata or validated against it at startup.
benefits: One generic engine replaces N hand-written mappers: read, insert, update and delete exist once and are driven by descriptors read out of the metadata.
Adding or renaming a mapped class changes metadata, not code - the engine stays closed for modification while the model stays open for extension.
The mapping becomes a machine-readable artifact: the same declaration can generate DDL or migrations, typed query APIs, documentation and serialization rules.
Cross-cutting mapping concerns - null handling, type conversion, generated keys, optimistic locking, lazy loading - are implemented once and applied uniformly instead of being repeated per class.
Schema and object model evolve independently: column/field divergence is absorbed by metadata declarations rather than by edits across every mapper.
Conventions supply defaults and explicit overrides stay local, so the ordinary class needs no mapping code at all while the exceptional case is still expressible.
tradeoffs: The metadata is a second schema: nothing prevents it from drifting from the real DDL, and drift surfaces as runtime failures - you must generate one from the other or validate at startup.
Indirection hides what actually runs: debugging a wrong column or a missing join means reading generated SQL and framework internals instead of code you wrote.
Reading metadata costs: runtime reflection or metadata walking adds startup time and per-operation overhead, which pushes teams towards caching, compiled models or code generation.
The framework's expressiveness is a ceiling: exotic types, database-specific SQL and irregular legacy schemas force escape hatches that partly defeat the metadata model.

Magic and coupling: what happens is invisible in the class, newcomers must learn the framework's conventions and precedence rules, and annotations or attributes tie domain classes to the persistence library.
Versioning: upgrading the mapping framework can change naming, nullability or fetch semantics, so a library upgrade becomes a mapping migration.

participants.responsibility: Declarative home of the object-relational correspondence - mapping files, code annotations or attributes, code-first table objects, struct tags or a schema definition - and the single source of truth for table, column, type and relationship knowledge.

Loads the store once (at startup, at compile time or at code-generation time) and turns it into mapping descriptors: field-to-column pairs, types, keys, generated values, relationships, inheritance and locking details.

Uses the descriptors to implement read, insert, update and delete for every mapped class, including SQL construction, parameter binding, result materialisation and identity handling; it contains no class-specific logic.
Plain class whose field names and types are the metadata's reference points; it carries no SQL and no mapping code, only domain data.
The tables and columns the metadata must agree with: generated from the metadata, validated against it at startup, or read out of the database by introspection or a code generator.

use_cases: A system with dozens of similarly shaped tables where hand-written data mappers would be repetitive: one mapping engine plus one metadata declaration per class.

Schema-first projects where the database already exists and the mapping should be derived from it by introspection or a code generator (EF Core reverse engineering, Rails schema introspection, SeaORM entity generation).
Framework and library builders who must let users map their own classes without shipping per-class code - an ORM, an object-document mapper or a serialization library.
Multi-database products in which only the dialect and type map of the metadata changes between targets while the domain classes stay identical.
Teams that want one declaration to drive several artifacts: DDL or migrations, typed query APIs, validation rules and documentation.

Hibernate ORM/Jakarta Persistence applications declare @Entity, @Table and @Column metadata; the provider builds a persistent metamodel and generic Session or EntityManager operations perform CRUD, so one declaration replaces per-entity mapper code.

EF Core applications combine conventions, data annotations and Fluent API configuration to build an entity model that drives LINQ translation and updates; explicit configuration pins renamed columns and relationships.

SQLAlchemy declarative mappings turn class attributes and mapped_column() declarations into Table and Mapper metadata; that metadata feeds SQL compilation and unit-of-work persistence, while imperative mapping keeps existing classes annotation-free.
avoid_when: Only a handful of classes with hand-written SQL that is already clear: a mapper per class, or row-to-object code inside a table data gateway, is simpler and easier to debug.
Active Record or Transaction Script territory: when the domain is essentially the table, generic metadata mapping buys nothing.
Legacy or irregular schemas in which every table's mapping is genuinely different - the metadata degenerates into a pile of per-case escape hatches.
Performance-critical bulk paths where SQL must be hand-tuned; bypassing the engine is possible but adds a second, unmanaged mapping to maintain.
No budget to keep metadata and schema in sync: drift is this pattern's characteristic failure mode, and no framework prevents it for you.
anti_patterns: Metadata as decoration: the annotations are present but a hand-written mapper still encodes the real mapping, so two sources of truth drift apart.
In-house ORM growth: the generic engine accumulates special cases for individual tables until it is harder to maintain than the code it replaced.
Reflecting per row: re-reading attributes or annotations inside the fetch loop instead of materialising descriptors once per class.
Annotations everywhere: the domain model imports the persistence library, so the mapping can no longer be swapped or unit-tested without touching every class.
Trusting conventions blindly: relying on inferred pluralisation or snake_case so that renaming a class silently changes the table or column it reads.
design_principles: Single source of truth: mapping knowledge lives in exactly one place and every other artifact is derived from it.
Open/closed: new mapped classes extend the system through metadata and registration while the engine stays closed for modification.
Persistence ignorance at the class level: the entity holds data, not SQL (the contrast to Active Record).
DRY at the mechanism level: repeated per-class code collapses into one engine, and repeated mapping declarations collapse into conventions plus explicit overrides.
Explicit precedence: conventions are defaults, overrides are explicit and local, and the order in which they win is documented.
best_practices: Declare the mapping once and derive as much as possible from it: DDL or migrations, typed queries, serialization and documentation.
Validate the metadata against the live schema at startup, or generate one from the other, so drift fails fast instead of at the first query.
Materialise descriptors once per class - cache them, use compiled models, or generate code - rather than re-reading annotations per operation.
Keep a documented escape hatch (raw SQL or a custom type handler) for what the metadata model cannot express, instead of growing the engine.
Treat mapping changes like schema changes: review them, version them and cover the tricky mappings with integration tests against a real database.
Prefer the ecosystem's canonical metadata form (annotations, mapping files, schema DSL) over a bespoke table nobody else can read.
